structure.title: Title, abstract and Section I Introduction
Section IV Trends and Evidence of Selection

observations.statement: The estimand is framed as a positive weighted average local treatment effect on compliers under a two-stage least squares randomized-judge design, citing the LATE framework directly.
The identification argument is organized around four named conditions for instrument validity, each addressed in its own labeled subsection with institutional and empirical support.

Exclusion is argued by checking that the instrument is only weakly correlated with other dimensions of judge discretion and that results are stable when controlling for an alternative stringency measure tied to judgment amounts.
Monotonicity is described in terms of complier behavior and checked with two empirical tests: nonnegative first-stage estimates across subsamples and a split-sample stringency cross-check.

The IV design is motivated explicitly by showing that simple cross-sectional and difference-in-differences comparisons are likely biased because of differential pre-filing trends between the treated and comparison groups.
Two court-record data sources are named with distinct sample periods for each city, and the unit of analysis is defined as the case-individual rather than the household.

Sample restrictions (business and condominium cases, missing identifiers, very large claimed damages, weeks with only one judge, minimum judge or courtroom caseloads) are each listed with the stated purpose of reducing noise in the instrument.
Use of restricted Census Bureau microdata is disclosed together with the disclosure-review and authorization process required before releasing statistics based on it.

Observation counts for the combined estimate are printed in brackets beneath the standard errors in the main results tables, with a pointer to an appendix table for counts of every subgroup and outcome.
Match rates for each administrative linkage are reported explicitly and benchmarked against match rates in closely related published studies that link similar identifiers.

Each outcome family (earnings, employment, residential mobility, homelessness-service use, credit-bureau measures, hospital visits) is defined with the specific administrative source and construction rule used to build it.
The treatment indicator is defined as a case ending with a court-issued eviction order, based on the last recorded outcome in the case history, with construction details deferred to an appendix.
The instrument is a leave-one-out mean eviction rate for the tenant's assigned judge or courtroom, computed within a given year and later residualized by court-year-quarter for visual presentation.

A composite financial-health index is built by standardizing each credit-bureau component on the nonevicted group's mean and standard deviation in the filing year, summing with sign conventions, and restandardizing.
Dollar-denominated outcomes are expressed in constant terms using a metro-area-specific price index rather than nominal values.
Main outcome tables stack a location-pooled combined estimate above location-specific and demographic-subgroup estimates, with parallel columns for two post-filing time horizons.
Table notes spell out the full baseline control set used in every specification and flag where an outcome family adds lagged-dependent-variable controls beyond the baseline set.
Every regression table states the standard-error type and the clustering level directly in its notes rather than only in the main text.
Each outcome table's first column reports the nonevicted-group mean as an interpretive benchmark placed directly beside the OLS and IV coefficient columns.

Standard errors are clustered at the judge or courtroom-by-year level throughout, matching the level at which the instrument varies, but this choice is stated in table notes without a dedicated paragraph arguing for it or discussing the number of clusters.
An explicit formula is given for computing the standard error of the equally weighted combined estimate across the two non-poolable location samples.
A dedicated first-stage table reports the instrument coefficient with and without controls and a partial F-statistic for each location, presented in the main text.

A balance table regresses both the treatment indicator and the instrument on observable case and tenant characteristics with a joint significance test, reported in the main text as the exogeneity check.

Monotonicity checks (nonnegative first-stage estimates across subsamples and a complementary split-sample stringency test) are summarized narratively in the main text with full tables placed in the online appendix.
observations.locator: Section V.A.2.iv, referencing Online Appendix Tables G.11-G.13

observations.statement: Pairwise correlations between the instrument and alternative dimensions of judge stringency, and a first-stage reestimation including those alternative measures, are reported in the online appendix as exclusion-restriction evidence.
observations.locator: Section V.A.2.iii, referencing Online Appendix Tables G.6-G.8

observations.statement: First-stage robustness to alternative sample-restriction choices, an alternative way of identifying the first judge, and additional controls for other judge-behavior dimensions is summarized in the main text with detail in a dedicated appendix subsection.
observations.locator: Section V.A.2.i, referencing Online Appendix G.A

observations.statement: Alternative definitions of a residential move, addressing possible undercount from missing address updates, are explored in an online appendix and summarized narratively in the main text.
observations.locator: Section VI.A.2, footnote referencing Online Appendix I

observations.statement: Earnings and employment estimates are checked separately for Great-Recession versus non-Great-Recession years, with the comparison reported only as a footnote pointer to appendix results.
observations.locator: Section VI.C, footnote referencing Online Appendix H.A

observations.statement: A symmetric difference-in-differences estimator is presented as an alternative to the IV design for interpreting effects on the average evicted tenant rather than only compliers, with the comparison summarized in the main text and developed fully in an appendix.
observations.locator: Section VI.G, referencing Online Appendix J

observations.statement: Subgroup breakdowns by gender and race are reported in every main results table, with the choice of subgroups justified ex ante by citing qualitative and discrimination-focused literature rather than presented as exploratory.
Formal tests of equality between subgroup coefficients are conducted but reported only via a pointer to an online appendix table rather than inline in the main results tables.
observations.locator: Section VI.C, referencing Online Appendix Table H.1

observations.statement: Homelessness results are framed both as an outcome of direct policy interest and as a possible intermediate mechanism through which eviction could later affect labor-market outcomes.
A near-null effect on destination-neighborhood poverty rates is used explicitly to argue against a change-in-neighborhood-environment mechanism for the other estimated effects.
Point estimates throughout the results section are routinely restated as a percentage of the nonevicted group's mean immediately next to the coefficient discussion.
Effects on the financial-health index are expressed in standard-deviation units and benchmarked against magnitudes reported in cited bankruptcy-relief and neighborhood-mobility studies.
Homelessness-service effects are translated into an aggregate back-of-envelope count of additional shelter users across the two study areas in a given year.
A small, statistically imprecise effect on destination-neighborhood poverty is interpreted through the width of its confidence interval rather than through the point estimate alone.

The authors state that mobility and homelessness estimates likely understate the true effect because outcomes are only observed for individuals named on the lease and unsheltered homelessness is not captured.

A limitation is noted that the paper's treatment, a court-ordered eviction, is conceptually narrower than the broader forced-move concept used in some prior sociology studies, limiting direct comparability of magnitudes.
General-equilibrium effects of eviction-related policy reforms are explicitly flagged as unsettled and outside what the paper's design can speak to.

Studying two large, institutionally distinct cities rather than one is framed explicitly as strengthening external validity relative to single-site prior work, with a dedicated figure comparing standardized estimates across the two locations.
A separate subsection addresses what can and cannot be inferred about the full evicted population, given that IV estimates identify effects only for compliers.

Trend figures around the filing date add the nonevicted group's omitted-period mean back into every plotted coefficient so that levels, not just relative changes, are directly interpretable regardless of the omitted period chosen.
A summary-statistics table compares the evicted group, the nonevicted group, and a neighborhood-matched renter benchmark side by side, reporting standard deviations in parentheses beneath each mean.

A cross-location scatterplot of standardized coefficients uses distinct marker shapes for IV versus OLS estimates and distinct colors or shapes for outcome groups to summarize consistency across settings.
A single significance-star convention at conventional thresholds is applied consistently across all regression tables in the paper.
The introduction previews the paper's main quantitative findings across housing, labor-market, financial, and health outcomes before the design and results sections are presented.

Institutional background and data description are placed before the identification strategy and results, and the introduction closes with an explicit roadmap paragraph describing the order of the remaining sections.

Detailed robustness, monotonicity, and exclusion-restriction material is concentrated in a lettered online appendix referenced repeatedly by pointer throughout the design and results sections rather than reproduced as in-text robustness subsections.
An explicit contribution paragraph in the introduction enumerates, in turn, how the paper's data, design, and scope extend a cited prior sociology literature on eviction.
A Data Availability statement at the end of the article names a Harvard Dataverse deposit with a DOI as the location of the analysis code underlying the article.

At least one administrative source is stated to be barred by a data-sharing agreement from being brought into the Census Research Data Center, illustrating a procedure-bound restriction on combining sources.

Each administrative data source used to build outcomes is named together with its custodial state or city agency, distinguishing government administrative records from any survey or commercial source.

concordance.paper_says: Two-stage least squares IV using the leave-one-out judge/courtroom stringency instrument, per equations (2)-(3)
concordance.card_shows: ivreghdfe and ivregress specs recorded as 2sls estimator (s2, s4), instrumenting eviction with stringency

concordance.paper_says: Court-by-year-quarter fixed effects included in all main IV and OLS specifications
concordance.card_shows: fe field recorded as null for the main IV specs (s1-s4); the code absorbs fixed effects via an unresolved macro variable rather than a literal FE list

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors clustered at the judge (courtroom)-year level in every main results table
concordance.card_shows: se cluster_level recorded as null for the main IV specs; the code clusters on an unresolved macro variable rather than a literal group name

concordance.paper_says: Clustered standard errors used throughout the main analysis

concordance.card_shows: controls recorded only as an unresolved macro variable reference in the specification line, without the underlying variable list

concordance.paper_says: No weighting scheme is described for the individual-level IV or OLS regressions
concordance.card_shows: weights field recorded as null for all specs

concordance.card_shows: a single diagnostic entry is recorded for first_stage with role unknown and no statistic value captured

concordance.paper_says: Sample restricted to ages 18-55 at filing, linked to earnings/employment records, with minimum judge or courtroom caseload thresholds and several case-type exclusions
concordance.card_shows: sample condition recorded only as an opaque indicator variable in the specification line, without the underlying restriction list

concordance.paper_says: Results are organized into eight main numbered tables and six numbered figures across the results and design sections
concordance.card_shows: outputs recorded with zero tables and zero figures extracted from the code

concordance.paper_says: Replication code and data availability statement point to a Harvard Dataverse deposit
concordance.card_shows: card extracted from a code directory matching the same Dataverse deposit identifier

concordance.paper_says: An extensive robustness program is described narratively (alternative sample restrictions, alternative move definitions, Great Recession subperiods, symmetric difference-in-differences comparison), mostly detailed in the online appendix
concordance.card_shows: no robustness-check records are present in the extracted card

gaps: No preregistration, pre-analysis plan, or IRB/consent statement was found anywhere in the main text or acknowledgments.
No paragraph beyond the table notes justifies clustering at the judge (courtroom)-year level or discusses the number of clusters as a potential concern.
No R-squared is reported in any main regression table.
No explicit multiple-testing adjustment is described despite reporting many outcomes and demographic subgroups across the results tables.

The paper's Online Appendix, referenced dozens of times for robustness, monotonicity, and exclusion-restriction detail, is hosted separately by the journal and is not part of this extracted text, so its exact content could not be verified directly and is summarized only through the paper's own in-text pointers.

reading.note: Read the entire extracted text sequentially in six large chunks covering lines 1-3151 (pages 1-65): title and abstract, Sections I-VII, the Data Availability statement, and the reference list (pages 59-64). Page 65 is an unrelated publisher advertisement (a Northwestern University prize call for nominations), not article content. The paper's Online Appendix, which the main text repeatedly points to for robustness checks, monotonicity tests, exclusion-restriction evidence, and additional outcome tables, is hosted separately by QJE and is not included in this text file, so no appendix pages could be read; all appendix-related observations rely on the paper's own main-text descriptions of that material.
